results.feedback: The submission is too generic and fails to meet the criteria for specificity, estimation, and reflection. To improve, you must: 1) Clearly define your specific role and industry. 2) Name specific processes or systems for each opportunity (e.g., 'Automating the invoice reconciliation process in the Finance team' rather than 'be more efficient'). 3) Provide a concrete estimate for the cost of inaction (e.g., £50,000 per year in manual labor or 200 hours of lost productivity). 4) Offer an honest assessment of the political or cultural barriers preventing action. 5) Explain why you would stake your reputation on one specific choice, citing its feasibility and potential impact. 6) Provide evidence of how you used AI to pressure-test these ideas.

This submission is significantly below the required standard. It fails to provide specific details regarding the learner's role, industry, or the particular systems and processes targeted for improvement. The opportunities listed are generic ('use AI to be more efficient') rather than named, context-specific initiatives. The cost of inaction is not estimated with any concrete figures or data, and the reasons for inaction ('it is hard') lack the necessary insight into organizational politics, capacity, or ownership. Additionally, the AI Lens section provides no evidence of pressure-testing or reflection. To pass, you must name specific teams or processes, provide a rough numerical cost of inaction, and honestly assess the non-technical barriers to change.

This submission is too generic and lacks the necessary detail to be considered a viable Opportunity Map. To improve, please specify your exact role and industry. Each opportunity must name a specific system, process, or team (e.g., 'The Q3 procurement workflow' rather than 'be more efficient'). You must also provide a concrete estimate for the cost of inaction (a real number or time-cost) and an honest assessment of the internal politics or ownership issues preventing progress. The AI lens section requires a reflection on how AI helped you find these opportunities and a comparison between AI's analytical capabilities and your own human judgement regarding company politics.

answers.Set Your Scope: I am Operations Manager for a 40-branch retail bank in Botswana, responsible for branch back-office processing (account opening, KYC refresh, loan document checks). Sector: retail banking.
answers.Map Opportunity One: Use document AI to pre-check KYC refresh packs before they reach the central team. Cost of inaction: about 1,900 packs a month are rejected for missing documents, roughly 950 staff hours and BWP 180,000 a year in rework. Nobody has acted because KYC sits between Compliance and Operations and neither wants to own a model that touches regulated files.
answers.Map Opportunity Two: For the Credit team, an AI assistant that drafts the first credit memo from the loan application. Cost of inaction: memo drafting averages 3.5 hours per SME loan, about 600 loans a year, delaying decisions by four days. Nobody has acted because the Head of Credit fears auditors will question AI-written memos.
answers.Map Opportunity Three: Stretch, outside my remit: Marketing could use branch transaction patterns to predict which SME customers are about to leave. Cost of inaction: we lost 210 SME accounts last year, about BWP 2.1m in deposits. Nobody has acted because Marketing has no data access agreement with Operations.
answers.Choose the One You Would Stake Your Repu: Opportunity One. I own the back-office process end to end and the rework cost is already in my budget line, so I can run a pilot in five branches without anyone else's approval. The Compliance concern is real, so the pilot keeps a human checker on every flagged pack.
answers.AI pressure-test and AI Lens: I asked an AI assistant to list overlooked automation opportunities in branch back-office work; it surfaced the credit memo idea I had not considered. I used it to sanity-check the BWP 180,000 estimate, which it put lower until I added the overtime rate. It could not tell me why Compliance resists ownership: that political read is mine, from two steering meetings this year.

results.feedback: An outstanding submission that meets all the criteria for a strong answer. You have provided specific, named opportunities within a clearly defined scope. The cost of inaction is estimated with concrete figures (1,900 packs, BWP 180,000, 210 accounts), which adds significant weight to the business case. Your analysis of why these opportunities have been ignored—specifically the political tension between Compliance and Operations and the fear of audit in Credit—shows the high-level 'political read' required of a transformation leader. The AI pressure-test is well-documented, showing a clear understanding of AI's utility in brainstorming and sanity-checking while acknowledging its limitations in navigating organizational politics.

This is an exemplary submission that hits every requirement of the rubric with high specificity. You have provided concrete, quantified costs of inaction (e.g., 950 staff hours, BWP 2.1m in deposits) which makes the business case compelling and actionable. Your 'political read' on why these opportunities remain unaddressed—specifically the ownership friction between Compliance and Ops and the Head of Credit's fear of auditors—demonstrates the sophisticated organizational awareness required of a Transformation Leader. The choice to stake your reputation on Opportunity One is well-reasoned, leveraging your own budget and authority to bypass typical corporate inertia. Finally, the AI Lens section clearly distinguishes between the technical utility of AI for estimation and the human judgment required for navigating office politics.

This is a model submission. You provided highly specific, localized opportunities within your banking context. Your cost-of-inaction estimates (BWP 180k rework, BWP 2.1m deposits) provide the necessary 'hard' evidence for transformation. Your political analysis of ownership gaps (Compliance vs. Ops) and cultural fears (Head of Credit/Auditors) demonstrates the 'Leader' aspect of the T4L rubric. The AI pressure-test effectively shows how you balanced tool-based ideation with local contextual knowledge.
